candidate.hook: Most meditation apps quietly teach dependence: the calm shows up when the chime does—and evaporates with your next notification.

candidate.payload:
Most guided apps train state calm as a cue-dependent behavior: relaxation is conditioned to a particular voice, timer, and phone context, so it fails to generalize when stress hits elsewhere (per Bouton 2002 on context-specific learning; see also context-dependent memory effects per Smith & Vela 2001). The product mechanics reinforce app use more than skill transfer—streaks and badges operate as variable-ratio reinforcement, keeping you returning for relief rather than tolerating sensations without it. In trials, app-based mindfulness shows small, short-term anxiety reductions that often attenuate after the intervention window—e.g., meta-analytic evidence for smartphone mental health apps reports modest effects (per Firth 2017), and single-app RCTs show immediate gains with unclear maintenance beyond guided use (e.g., Headspace reduces stress over 10 sessions in Economides 2018; workplace app use improves well-being in Bostock 2019). Meanwhile, many modules emphasize soothing over interoceptive exposure, so users get better at escaping uncomfortable sensations rather than updating threat predictions—exactly the opposite of inhibitory learning that sustains long-term anxiety change (per Craske et al. 2014).

If you want stability between sessions, practice without audio and off-phone, eyes open, across varied places/postures/times, and at different arousal levels so the skill isn’t tied to a single context. Add brief, frequent reps in real life (three-breath check-ins, labeling, 4-6 paced breathing) and include mild, planned provocations (a brisk stair climb, a cold rinse, sitting with a surge) to build tolerance to internal cues. Track between-session metrics—how fast you recover from a spike, how many urges you ride out—rather than streaks. The goal is not bigger “calm hits,” but a nervous system that updates and holds steady without the chime.
